title: Hello, my name is Ani
title_target: नमस्ते, मेरा नाम आनी है — namaste, meraa naam aanii hai
goal: Greet people, say your name, ask how someone is, and meet one small word you can never leave out of a Hindi sentence: है.
bekal: greet with नमस्ते and answer it
say your name with मेरा नाम … है
choose between आप, तुम, and तू
use जी to sound polite with no effort

dialogs.title: संवाद — At the door of the boarding house
dialogs.intro: Ani has just moved into a boarding house in Delhi. Her neighbor Rahul greets her on the stairs. Notice one thing from the very first line: almost every sentence ends in है or हूँ — and a Hindi sentence is never complete without it.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.literal: hello — ji. my — name — Ani — is.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: I'm fine, thank you. And you?
lines.literal: I — fine — am, thanks. and — you?

lines.speaker: राहुल:
lines.id: I'm fine too. Are you from Indonesia?
lines.literal: I — also — fine — am. you — Indonesia — from — are?

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.literal: ji — yes. I — Jakarta — from — am.

lines.speaker: राहुल:
lines.id: Very good. This is my sister, Priya.
lines.literal: very — good. this — my(fem.) — sister — is, Priya.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: Me too. Do you all live here?
lines.literal: to-me — also. you — people — here — living — are?

lines.speaker: राहुल:
lines.id: Yes, we live right here. See you!
lines.literal: ji — yes, we — right-here — living — are. again — will-meet!

notes: **है is the word beginners misplace or drop — and it can never go missing.** English has *is/am/are* too, but Hindi puts it **at the very end**, after everything else: मेरा नाम आनी **है** — "my name Ani is". Without है the sentence is not just odd; it isn't a sentence yet.

**नमस्ते works for hello and goodbye**, morning and night — one word for every occasion, no *good morning/good evening* to choose from. For something slightly more formal, use **नमस्कार**. Among Urdu speakers and Indian Muslims the greeting is **आदाब** (*aa-daab*) or **अस्सलामु अलैकुम**; among Sikhs, **सत श्री अकाल**. Each is answered with the very same words.

**जी is the most important word in Hindi that means nothing.** It sticks to everything to soften the sentence: **जी हाँ** (yes), **जी नहीं** (no), **राहुल जी** (Mr. Rahul), or on its own as "yes?" when someone calls you. Adding जी is almost never wrong; leaving it out can sound cold. ⚠️ With older people and new acquaintances, use जी.

**कैसी हैं, not कैसे हैं — because Ani is a woman.** This is your first sign of something that will change how you think: in Hindi, **the person's gender goes into the words**. To a woman: *आप कैसी हैं?* To a man: *आप कैसे हैं?* The answer follows suit — Ani says *मैं ठीक हूँ* (safe for both), but to say "I'm tired" she must say *मैं थकी हूँ*, while Rahul says *मैं थका हूँ*. Unit 4 covers this in full.

**There are three ways to say "you", and choosing the wrong one really shows.** **आप** for anyone older, new, or respected — the form used throughout this course. **तुम** for friends your age and people you are close to. **तू** for very close friends, small children, and prayer; to a stranger it sounds rude. ⚠️ As a newcomer, use **आप** with everyone. Nobody is offended by too much respect.

**यह is spelled "yah" but said "yeh".** The same goes for **वह** (spelled *vah*, said **voh**). This is not a quirk of two words but the pattern you read about at the front of the book: a **ह** squeezed between sounds changes the color of the vowels around it. This course always prints what is **said**, not a letter-by-letter spelling.

**शुक्रिया or धन्यवाद?** Both mean thank you. **शुक्रिया** (from the same Arabic root as *shukr*, gratitude) sounds warm and everyday; **धन्यवाद** is more formal and more often written than spoken. ⚠️ A cultural surprise: Indians **thank people for small things far less often** than English speakers do. Thanking your mother for cooking, or a close friend for pouring tea, actually sounds distant. Save शुक्रिया for strangers and for real kindness.

grammars.title: होना — the first verb you need
body: होना (*ho-naa*, "to be") is the verb you will use most. Learn this table today; half of all A1 sentences are built on it.
after: To negate, just put **नहीं** right before है: *मैं ठीक नहीं हूँ* (I'm not fine). ⚠️ In fast speech है often drops after नहीं — *मैं ठीक नहीं* — but don't copy that yet; write it in full until the pattern sticks.

⚠️ **आप always takes हैं, even when you are talking to just one person.** Hindi shows respect through the plural — exactly like French *vous*. The same goes for parents you talk about: *पिता जी घर पर हैं* (Father is at home), not है.

grammars.title: Greetings, goodbyes, and small talk

head: हिंदी
Pronunciation
When to use it
rows: more formal; common on air and in speeches
Urdu speakers' greeting; polite and warm
how are you — to a man
how are you — to a woman

after: ⚠️ **अलविदा is not "see you".** It is for real farewells — moving to another city or country, or a sad scene in a film. For everyday goodbyes, **नमस्ते** or **फिर मिलेंगे** is enough.

blocks.text: These four sentences cover a whole first introduction. Learn them as one block, swap in your own details, and you have an introduction ready for any occasion.

head: Sentence
Pronunciation
Meaning
rows: मुझे हिंदी थोड़ी थोड़ी आती है।
mu-jhe hin-dii tho-Rii tho-Rii aa-tii hai

blocks.title: Two answers that will save you in week one
items: **मुझे हिंदी नहीं आती।** (*mu-jhe hin-dii na-hiiⁿ aa-tii*) — "I don't speak Hindi." It sounds far better than silence, and it almost always makes the other person slow down.
**ज़रा धीरे बोलिए।** (*za-raa dhii-re bo-li-ye*) — "Please speak a little more slowly." **ज़रा** means "a little" and makes any request sound polite. Keep this one handy; you'll use it every day.

⚠️ Don't answer the compliment *आप हिंदी बोलती हैं!* with a flat denial. The natural reply is **थोड़ी थोड़ी** (a little) or **सीख रही हूँ** (I'm learning). Denying it outright just stops the conversation.

blocks.text: One thing about names. Indians will ask your name and then, quite often, ask **आपका शुभ नाम?** (*aap-kaa shubh naam* — "your good name?"). It isn't a different question; it's the polite way of asking the same thing. Just give your name. And don't be surprised if your name is repeated with a slightly different pronunciation — not every sound travels neatly into Hindi, and people are trying, just like you.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right form of होना: हूँ, है, हैं, or हो.
Choose कैसे or कैसी, depending on who you're talking to.
items: To an old gentleman: आप ____ हैं?

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order. Remember: the verb goes last.

answers: मेरा नाम आनी है। — मैं जकार्ता से हूँ। — आप कैसे हैं? — यह मेरी बहन है। — हम यहाँ रहते हैं।
नमस्ते! मेरा नाम बुदी है। — मैं इंडोनेशिया से हूँ। — आप कैसी हैं? — मैं ठीक हूँ, शुक्रिया। — यह मेरा भाई है। — फिर मिलेंगे!
